Load packages

Code 
library(here) # Project relative paths
library(dplyr) # Data wrangling
library(sf) # Working with spatial features
library(terra) # Working with rasters
library(ggplot2) # Make a plot

Overview

So far, we have focused on mapping vector and raster data. This exercise will focus on conducting raster analyses using built-in and custom functions.

Learning objectives

  • Apply functions to rasters
  • Write custom functions for raster analyses
  • Perform raster time-series analyses
  • Extract and summarize raster values by polygons
  • Visualize spatial and temporal trends

Introduction

The terra package is powerful and efficient at analyzing raster and vector spatial data. It provides tools for importing, manipulating, visualizing, and exporting large geospatial datasets while optimizing memory usage and computational performance. For raster analysis, terra supports common operations such as extraction, cropping, masking, resampling, reclassification, focal (neighborhood) analyses, terrain calculations, and raster algebra. This exercise will focus on using built-in terra functions as well as custom function for analyzing raster data.

Exercise 1: Extract and analyze raster data

Here, we’ll use the extract function to extract model predictions (predicted day of year) from the precise location where lilac observations were collected (observed day of year). This allows us to further compare the two datasets.

Use code from previous exercises to import the lilac_2018_model raster (model predictions of leaf out) and the phenometric data for lilac leaf out (observed dates of leaf out).

Code 
# Use the 'rast()' function to import the raster
lilacModel_r <- rast(here("data", "lilac_2018_model.tiff"))

# Phenometric data (shapefile produced in previous exercise)
lilacObs_sf <- st_read(here("data", "lilac_2018_obs.shp"))

  using driver `ESRI Shapefile'

The extract() function in terra extracts predictions from location data, including sf point files. The first argument is the raster, the second the locations.

Code 
# Extract model predictions for each observation location
lilacObs_extr <- extract(lilacModel_r, lilacObs_sf)

Sometimes it’s easier to work with the results in a data frame, which we’ll do below. By default, terra names the extracted data as layer, so we’ll make the column name more informative (leaf_doy).

Code 
lilacObs_extr <- lilacObs_extr %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rename("leaf_doy" = "layer")

Next, we can estimate the extent to which the model under-predicts vs. over-predicts the date of lilac leaf out by subtracting the leaf_doy columns.

Code 
# Differences (in days) between predicted and observed lilac leaf out
differences <- lilacObs_extr$leaf_doy- lilacObs_sf$leaf_doy

Create a histogram of differences using the hist() function in base R. It might be helpful to define a sequence of breaks.

Code 
hist(differences, breaks = seq(-250, 50, 25))

Now calculate some simple summary statistics of the differences.

Code 
# Mean
mean(differences)
[1] -13.7887
Code 
# Range
range(differences)
[1] -237.0205   48.0000
Code 
# Median
median(differences)
[1] 0.3383713

Question 1 What information do your simple analyses provide that can’t be seen on a map? Overall, what do the results say about the performance of the model for lilac leaf out?

Answer: On average, predicted dates were 13.71 days earlier (range = -237 to 48 days) than observed dates, which suggests that the model is under-predicting the date of lilac leaf out. However, the extreme outliers are likely due to observer error. The model actually seems to perform pretty well if we reduce the impact of outliers by calculating the median difference, which is only 1 day.

Exercise 2: Apply custom functions to raster data

Custom functions allow us to:

  • Avoid repeating code
  • Improve readability
  • Increase reproducibility
  • Apply the same workflow to many rasters
  • Simplify complex analyses

(1) Evaluating temperature anomalies

We’ll move on from the lilac modeling data set to climate change. Specifically, well ask this question: for each year between 2020 and 2024, which OR counties experienced the largest July temperature anomalies relative to the 30-year average?

Data preparation

We will use three data sets:

  1. Tmax for July for 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024 (5 rasters)
  2. Average Tmax for July between 1981-2010 (1 raster)
  3. U.S. county simple features (sf) object

Below a list of raster files for July in individual years is created, plus the 30-year average file.

Take a peek at the raster data - there are 872,505 raster cell values

Code 
Jul_30yrAv <- rast(Jul_30yrAv_fl)

plot(Jul_30yrAv)

Import the county boundary data (counties.shp) and filter out counties for OR.

Code 
# US counties feature
counties <- st_read(here("data", "counties.shp"))

Function: temperature anomaly by county

The top_county_func function determines which Oregon counties had the largest difference in July temperature compared to the 30 year average. The n argument defines the top number of counties with the largest anomaly to return.

Apply the function across years

Use lapply to apply the function across 1:length(July_fls).

results <- lapply(1:length(Jul_fls), top_county_func)

(2) Direction of change in annual Tmax

How has annual maximum temperature (Tmax) changed across Oregon between 1990 and 2019?

Load annual data.

Code 
USA_fls <- list.files(
  here("data", "prism_data", "annual"),
  pattern = ".bil$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

Function: regression model of Tmax

The slope_func function below loads, crops, and subsets annual Tmax rasters and then runs a regression model for each raster grid cell. The results will provide insight into the direction of change in annual Tmax for each decade.

Code 
slope_func <- function(years) {
  
  # Get rasters and crop to OR, and retain layers of corresponding years
  USA_r <- rast(USA_fls)
  
  # Crop the raster data
  OR_r <- crop(
    USA_r,
    ext(-124.7294, -116.2949, 41.7150, 46.4612)
  )
  
  # Subset raster layer for the year range
  OR_r <- OR_r[[years]]
  
  # Run a regression model for each cell of the raster stack
  rm <- regress(
    OR_r,
    1:nlyr(OR_r),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
   return(rm)
}

Analyze the trend of annual Tmax for each decade.

Code 
# Decades
year_sets <- list(
  1:10, # 1990-1999
  11:20, # 2000-2010
  21:30 # 2011-2020
)

Apply the function below.

Code 
slopes <- lapply(year_sets, slope_func)

Take a look at the trend results. What does each list element correspond to?

For increased clarity, we can rename the list elements. These can be used for titles for creating basic plots in terra.

Code 
names(slopes) <- c( "OR_1990_1999",  "OR_2000_2010",  "OR_2011_2020")

Let’s look at the results. Annual Tmax exhibited different trends throughout OR if we look at each decade separately, but temperatures are generally increasing in many areas. The x layer in each raster corresponds to the slope - i.e., the trend in annual Tmax for the respective time periods. We can plot these results by referencing the second layer for each list element.

Practice 2 Modify the trend function

4. Change the extent to a different state.

5. Change the time frame to a longer period, such as 20 or 30 years.

Visualize the Tmax trends by Oregon county for 2011-2020. Here we convert countiesOR to a SpatVector format, which is designed for vector data in the terra package. You can save the results as a polygon and easily plot the results. By default, the output column name is x.

Code 
# Convert the sf feature to a SpatVector
countiesOR_v <- vect(countiesOR)

# Calculate zonal stats
slope_zonal <- zonal(slopes[[3]][[2]], countiesOR_v, 
                     fun = "mean", as.polygons = TRUE)

# Plot
plot(slope_zonal, y = "x", 
     plg=list(title="Zonal mean"))

Practice 3 Make a nicer plot

6. Practice your ggplot2 mapping skills to make a nicer map! (Hint: the data is countiesOR_z and values are mean). A nice addition could be a title like “Mean Rate of Tmax Change in Oregon (2011-2020)”, and you can visualized county names using geom_sf_text().

Code 
# Bind the mean value column to the OR counties feature
countiesOR_z <- bind_cols(countiesOR, mean = slope_zonal$x)

# Make a ggplot
ggplot(data = countiesOR_z) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = mean), color = "white", size = 0.2) +
  geom_sf_text(aes(label = name), size = 1.5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Zonal Mean") + # Clean, continuous color palette
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Rate of Tmax Change in Oregon (2011-2020)"
  )

Wrap up

We focused on using terra to extract and analyze raster and vector data. The package is large and extensive, with dozens (or hundreds!) of functions, and an ability to do parallel processing to speed up operations. Thus, it’s very powerful and an integral to working with rasters in R.

Potentially useful tutorials, free books, etc.
